Samsung's One UI 9 Is Bad News for Android Auto Users, Google Has the Good News
6 photos
Photo: Bogdan Popa/autoevolution
Samsung users have been battling Android Auto issues for as long as anyone can remember, and every single new Galaxy flagship ended up hitting the same connectivity problems . This time, it’s different. The connectivity problems aren’t caused by a new-generation smartphone but by a new-generation software update.
Samsung recently started rolling out One UI 9, the company’s latest and greatest software update that includes the update to Android 17 . Unsurprisingly, many users rushed to update their devices, as One UI 9 brings so many great configurations that all these users didn’t even care about the potential problems they could end up struggling with in their cars.
It turns out these problems are no longer potential but actually certain. Several users have been complaining that Android Auto doesn’t load after the update to One UI 9, and several others confirmed the same behavior in their cars.
Android Auto worked perfectly on One UI 8.5, many users revealed, but no longer fires up after the installation of the newly-released One UI 9.
In those rare cases where the app actually launches, Android Auto crashes in the middle of the drive due to what appears to be a connection loss.
The issues have already been reported with both wired and wireless connections, so while a random disconnect or a broken connection is typically caused by a bad cable, this isn’t the case here. Furthermore, users claim they’re using the same cord as they did before the update when everything was working correctly, so it wouldn’t make sense for the connection problems to be caused by a bad cord.
Users have already tried the typical workarounds in the Android Auto world, all to no avail. Clearing the cache of the Android Auto app, reinstalling it, and updating to the latest version doesn’t improve the experience, so many of these users are stuck with premium Android phones running the latest software versions without being able to run Android Auto.
Photo: Bogdan Popa/autoevolution Google: A fix is now available for One UI 9 users While a Google Community Specialist previously confirmed that reports of connection problems after the One UI 9 update had already been forwarded to the Android Auto team, it now looks like a fix is available.
Google has reportedly confirmed that the patch is now rolling out to Samsung phones running One UI 9, with the company promising that the issue will be fixed on all devices shortly.
The most recent Android Auto version is 18.1 . It started rolling out earlier this week through the Google Play Store, so if you don’t want to wait to get your hands on it - which could take up to several weeks - you can download and install it manually.
Photo: Bogdan Popa/autoevolution Big updates coming to Android Auto While Samsung users are eager to install new updates because they just want Android Auto to work, others have different reasons to be excited when new versions come out.
Android Auto is expected to receive the internally known as Cielo, the first major update since the introduction of Coolwalk in 2023 . With Cielo, Android Auto will get support for screens of all sizes, shapes, and resolutions, using the available screen estate more efficiently.
In terms of features, Android Auto will get support for widgets, and the long-term goal is to allow any widget that exists on Android phones to also become available in the car. Widgets will be displayed side-by-side with the rest of the Android Auto UI - and not on a separate screen, as it’s the case with CarPlay - and will allow users to get quick information, such as weather details and the next calendar appointments, without having to launch the full apps.
Photo: Bogdan Popa/autoevolution Android Auto will also unlock two new app categories: video apps and browsers. YouTube will pioneer the debut of video apps on Android Auto, allowing users to watch videos on their infotainment screens when their cars are stationary. The video playback will be restricted when vehicles start moving, and if the apps support it, an audio-only mode will automatically kick in.
This system should allow uninterrupted playback behind the wheel without causing the video to become a major source of distraction. For YouTube, the audio-only mode would require a Premium subscription, as it’ll use the ability to play audio in the background, a feature that is not part of the free tier.
Google hasn’t yet provided an ETA as to when all these new features could land, but the company recently reiterated that they would become available soon . The consensus is that the first beta users could get them by the end of the year, while the production rollout would start in the first quarter of 2027 and continue throughout the rest of the year. By the summer, we should all be able to watch YouTube videos on our Android Auto screens.
